summary: Describes Zstandard (zstd), a lossless data compression mechanism, and registers a media type, a content encoding and a structured syntax suffix for carrying zstd data in MIME. Despite the name, the document is informational and the format is not an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Zstandard shrinks files so they take less space and travel faster, then restores them perfectly. This document describes it and gives it official names so web and email software can label compressed content.

questions: what is the zstd magic number
subtitle: A fast lossless compression format, and the media type and HTTP content coding that name it.

tldr.problem: Programs wanted a modern lossless compression format they could write down precisely, and a standard way to label zstd-compressed data when it travels in MIME and HTTP payloads.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the Zstandard frame and block format, which combines Huffman coding and Finite State Entropy coding with back-references into earlier data, and registers application/zstd, the zstd content coding and the +zstd suffix.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational, not an Internet Standards Track specification, despite the word standard in the name. It obsoletes RFC 8478 and has since been updated by RFC 9659.

today: RFC 8878 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 8478, and it has been updated by RFC 9659. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

sections.title: What Zstandard Is and Is Not
sections.content:
Zstandard, or zstd (pronounced "zee standard"), is a lossless data compression mechanism, akin to gzip (RFC 1952). This document describes the format and registers a media type, a content encoding and a structured syntax suffix so that zstd-compressed content can be labelled when it is carried in a payload.

The RFC warns readers twice that, despite the word "standard" in the name, it is not an Internet Standards Track specification. It is published for informational purposes only.

The format is defined to be independent of the CPU type, operating system, file system and character set, and to suit both file compression and pipe or streaming compression. Data can be produced or consumed using only an a priori bounded amount of intermediate storage, even for an arbitrarily long input stream. It does not attempt to allow random access to compressed data. A reference implementation written in portable C is cited.
sections.plainLanguage: Zstandard is like a vacuum bag for files: it shrinks them to save space and puffs them back out exactly as they were. The name sounds official, but this document is just a description, not a rulebook for the whole Internet.

sections.title: Frames, Headers and Blocks
sections.content:
Zstandard data is made of one or more frames. Each frame is independent, and the decompressed content of several concatenated frames is simply the concatenation of each frame's content. Two frame formats exist: Zstandard frames, which carry compressed data, and skippable frames, which carry custom user metadata.

A Zstandard frame starts with a 4-byte Magic_Number with the value 0xFD2FB528 (little-endian), then a Frame_Header of 2 to 14 bytes, then one or more data blocks, then an optional 4-byte Content_Checksum. The checksum is the low 4 bytes of an XXH64 hash of the original data with a seed of zero. The header tells the decoder, among other things, the Window_Size (the minimum buffer needed to decode, at least 1 KB), an optional dictionary ID and an optional decompressed size. Decoders are recommended to support window sizes up to 8 MB, and encoders are recommended not to produce frames that need more.

Each block has a 3-byte Block_Header with a last-block bit, a 2-bit block type and a 21-bit block size. A block is raw (stored as is), RLE (one byte repeated) or compressed. The block type value 3 is reserved, and a compliant decoder must reject it as corrupt data. A block's content is limited to the smaller of Window_Size and 128 KB. If a compressed block would be larger than the uncompressed one, sending a raw block is recommended.

Skippable frames begin with a magic number from 0x184D2A50 to 0x184D2A5F, then a 4-byte size and the user data. A decoder just skips them.
sections.plainLanguage: A compressed file is like a box of smaller boxes. Each box has a label on the front that says how big it is and whether it is the last one. Some boxes are just stuffed with your own notes, and the reader simply walks past those.

sections.title: How Compressed Blocks Work
sections.content:
A compressed block has two parts: a literals section and a sequences section. Literals are bytes that are stored directly. They can be raw, a single repeated byte, or Huffman-coded using 1 or 4 streams. When there are 4 streams, a 6-byte jump table gives the compressed sizes of the first three.

The sequences section is a list of commands. Each sequence says to copy a number of literals to the output and then to copy a match of some length from data that was already decoded, a given offset back. Three symbol types (literal length codes, offset codes and match length codes) are interleaved in one bitstream. For each, a compression mode says whether to use a predefined table, a single repeated symbol, a transmitted table, or the table from the previous block.

Two entropy coders do the bit-level work. Huffman coding is used for literals. FSE (Finite State Entropy, based on asymmetric numeral systems) is used for all other symbols and for the Huffman headers. FSE and Huffman bitstreams are read backwards, from the end of the stream to the beginning.

The three most recent offsets are remembered as repeat offsets, so that a short offset value of 1 to 3 can reuse them. For the first block they start as 1, 4 and 8, unless a dictionary supplies other values.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor says things like "write these letters, then copy the last few words you wrote" instead of repeating them. It also gives common pieces shorter codes, like using a single emoji-sized nickname for a long name.

sections.title: Dictionaries
sections.content:
A dictionary is data both sides already have, used as a pretend "past" in front of the data being compressed, so that small inputs can still find matches. Dictionaries are not included in the compressed content. The frame's Dictionary_ID says which one to use, but the RFC does not describe how a dictionary is obtained.

Raw content dictionaries are allowed and must be at least 8 bytes. Dictionaries made by zstd --train in the reference implementation have a format starting with the 4-byte magic number 0xEC30A437, a 4-byte Dictionary_ID (never 0), entropy tables, three repeat offsets and then the content.

Dictionary IDs at or below 32767, and at or above 231, are reserved for dictionaries registered with IANA. Other values can be used by private arrangement. Because the dictionary mechanism for MIME was still being explored, content labelled with the media type registered here should not use a dictionary.
sections.plainLanguage: A dictionary is a cheat sheet that the sender and the receiver both already have. Instead of spelling out common words, the sender just points at the cheat sheet.

sections.title: Registrations: Media Type, Content Coding and Suffix
sections.content:
IANA updated two existing registrations and made one new one. The media type application/zstd identifies a block of data compressed with zstd. It is binary, uses the file extension zst and has the magic number 0xFD2FB528.

The HTTP content coding named zstd was added to the HTTP Content Coding Registry, described as a stream of bytes compressed using the Zstandard protocol. The structured syntax suffix +zstd was registered for media types whose content is zstd-compressed.

No dictionary registry was requested, because the RFC states there are no dictionaries published for public use at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: This part gives zstd three official name tags: one for files, one for web transfers and one that other file types can add on the end of their names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like any compression method, zstd reduces redundancy, and the usual precautions apply. A message whose content must stay secret should never be compressed together with content generated by a third party, because that can be used to guess the secret by looking at the size change. The RFC cites the CRIME attack as an example.

Decoders must be hardened. Corrupted frames must not trigger reads or writes beyond allowed memory ranges, and the RFC singles out a bad Number_of_Sequences and a Frame_Content_Size smaller than the real output. Fuzz-testing is highly recommended. A decoder must also limit memory use, since an attacker can send well-formed frames with unreasonable memory requirements.

Third-party dictionaries may interact unexpectedly with a decoder and could enable memory or other resource-exhaustion attacks. Finally, skippable frames can carry arbitrary data and so can be used as a watermark to track a payload. Users worried about this should scan for such frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Zipping a secret together with something an attacker controls can leak hints about the secret. Readers also need to be careful not to open boxes that claim to need an impossible amount of room.

fields.name: Last_Block
fields.desc: Set when this is the last block; the frame ends after it.

fields.name: Block_Size
fields.desc: Size of the block content, or the repeat count for an RLE block.

items.label: Compressed_Block
items.desc: Literals and sequences, as described in the RFC.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Not a block; decoders must reject it as corrupt data.
